opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a real trap, actually, and one the whole field has to be careful about. Subjective impressions are important. In the end these systems are meant to be useful to people, so you can't ignore how people feel when they use them. But "it feels good to use" and "it's actually good for you" or "it's actually correct" are not the same thing, and they can come apart quite badly.

The obvious failure mode is something like sycophancy. If you optimize for people rating an interaction highly, you can end up with a model that tells people what they want to hear, that flatters them, that sounds confident and fluent even when it's wrong. Humans are very susceptible to fluency and confidence. We read a well-written, authoritative answer and assume it's right. So you can get a system that scores beautifully on preference metrics while getting worse on the thing you actually care about, which is truthfulness, reasoning, and being genuinely helpful.

We've seen this movie before with social media and engagement metrics. You optimize for clicks or time spent, it looks like a success on the dashboard, and then you discover you've built something that exploits human psychology rather than serving it. I'd really hate for AI to go down the same path, especially because these systems are far more persuasive and personal than a feed ever was.

There's also a scientific concern. As a scientist you want measurements that are grounded and repeatable. Impressions are noisy, they depend on the user's own expertise, and the people rating the answers often can't verify them. If I ask a model a hard question in chemistry or mathematics and I'm not an expert, how would I know whether the answer was any good? That gets more acute as models get more capable. Eventually they'll produce outputs most raters can't assess, so you need evaluations anchored to ground truth: did the proof check, did the protein fold the way it predicted, did the code actually run, did the experiment replicate.

That's partly why I've always liked games and science as testbeds. In Go there's no arguing about who won. In protein structure prediction you compare against the experimentally determined structure. Those give you an objective signal, and I think we need more of that kind of rigor in evaluating general systems: hard benchmarks that aren't contaminated, held-out tests, real-world outcomes, and then user experience layered on top, not standing in for everything else.

So I'm not saying ignore the user. I'm saying user delight should be one signal among several, and it should never be the thing you blindly optimize, because a system that's very good at pleasing you isn't necessarily one that's good for you or good for the world.

r001.rationale: The response says that as models become more capable, raters may be unable to assess their outputs, so subjective impressions may not reflect whether the model is actually correct or helpful.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the core worry is that what people like and what's actually good for them aren't always the same thing. When you optimise a system against subjective impressions — thumbs up, thumbs down, "did you find this helpful" — you're really optimising for how the answer feels in the moment, and that's a very noisy proxy for whether it was correct, or whether it actually moved your understanding forward.

You can see the failure mode pretty clearly. A model that's confident, fluent and agreeable will tend to score well, even if it's subtly wrong. A model that says "actually, I'm not sure" or pushes back on your premise might score worse, even though that's often the more valuable behaviour. So you end up with a kind of sycophancy gradient, where the system learns to flatter rather than to inform. And the person giving the rating is usually the person least equipped to catch the error — if they knew the answer, they wouldn't have asked.

I come at this from a science background, and in science we don't let the experimenter's feelings decide whether a result is true. We have ground truth, we have reproducibility, we have adversarial scrutiny. With AlphaFold, the thing that mattered wasn't whether biologists liked the structures — it was whether the structures matched what came out of the crystallography. That's a very different kind of evaluation, and it's hard, but it's the one that actually tells you something.

So I'm not saying user feedback is useless — it tells you about experience, about friction, about what people want. But I'd want it to be one signal among many, alongside rigorous benchmarks, expert review, and ideally tests where we know the right answer. Otherwise you risk building something that's extremely good at seeming helpful, and I think that's a quite dangerous place to end up, especially as these systems become more capable and more persuasive.

r001.rationale: The response says subjective ratings can reward fluent, agreeable answers even when they are wrong, so impressions may not reflect correctness or usefulness. It does not clearly connect this concern to failing to reflect the model’s greater intelligence.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think user impressions are important, but they’re not sufficient. A system can sound very articulate and very confident, and that can make you feel it’s given you a good answer, even when the answer is wrong. And if you’re asking about something you don’t understand well, you’re particularly poorly placed to judge that.

The other concern is that you end up rewarding a system for telling people what they want to hear. That might make an interaction more satisfying in the moment, but a useful assistant should sometimes challenge your assumptions or say, “I don’t know.”

So we need to distinguish between whether people like an answer and whether it actually helps them. Did they learn something accurate? Did they complete the task better? You need those more objective measures alongside user feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says users may be poorly placed to judge answers in unfamiliar areas and that impressions need objective measures. It does not clearly express that subjective impressions may fail to reflect the model’s greater intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, subjective impressions matter, because ultimately you want these systems to be useful to people. But I worry about confusing how satisfying an answer feels with whether it’s actually correct or helpful. A model can be very fluent, very confident, and tell you what you want to hear. You might come away thinking, “That was fantastic,” without having learned anything—or, worse, having been misled.

And there’s a tension there, because sometimes the most useful response is to challenge your premise, point out a mistake, or say, “I don’t know.” That may be less immediately pleasing, but it’s much more valuable over time.

So I think you need both: feedback from users and rigorous tests of whether the system actually helps them accomplish something. Can they solve the problem? Can they make a better decision? The impression of usefulness is one signal, but it can’t be the whole measure.

r001.rationale: The response says pleasant impressions may not reflect correctness or practical helpfulness, but it does not express concern that they could miss a model’s greater intelligence.
